contributions: identification and rigorous empirical validation of 'The First is The Best': a model's first-generated reasoning solution is optimal in up to 93.7% of cases, while subsequent alternative solutions rarely correct errors (75.4-82.8% failure rate) and can actively mislead a correct first solution into an incorrect one (up to 21.2% of cases), challenging the widely-accepted assumption that more test-time exploration is uniformly beneficial

the Forest of Errors (FoE) framework, formally modeling reasoning errors as a forest structure with quantifiable static and dynamic (reproduction-rate) metrics, plus a theoretical probabilistic-branching-process proof that FoE growth explains why the first solution is optimal

five empirical observations characterizing FoE dynamics: root-node correction (not descendant correction) decelerates error propagation; First's forest is smaller and grows slower than Subs'; joint high entropy AND high entropy variance (not either alone) predicts error-node genesis; and LRM self-reflection largely fails to prune FoE, with fake correction and refusal to correct dominating in later solutions

RED, a self-guided efficient-reasoning framework combining classifier-free-guidance-style negative-prompt intervention at entropy-flagged root-error-prone segments within the first solution, with complete discarding of subsequent solutions via a dual-consistency-gated early-stopping probe -- achieving up to 19.0% accuracy gains and 37.7-70.4% token reduction across six backbones and five benchmarks, and directly reducing FoE metrics 41.0-68.0% (versus a competing RL baseline's negligible 3.4-7.4% reduction)
limitations: A potential limitation of RED is the introduction of additional latency from the extra operations (periodic probing, entropy-based intervention) within the decoding process; the paper's own rigorous worst-case profiling shows this overhead averages only 4.6%, which the authors argue is comfortably outweighed by the time saved from early exit, yielding a net speedup, but it is nonetheless flagged as a limitation of the approach's decoding-time complexity.
method: First empirically establishes 'The First is The Best': comparing the model's first-generated solution (First) against subsequent solutions (Subs) across five LRMs and AIME25/GPQA-Diamond, First is optimal (uniquely correct or more robust than Subs) in up to 93.7% of cases; when First is wrong, Subs fails to correct it in 75.4-82.8% of cases; alarmingly, Subs actively misleads a correct First toward an incorrect answer in up to 21.2% of cases; and even when both are correct, Subs retains latent instability risk under resampling. To explain this, models errors within a reasoning path as a Forest of Errors (FoE): using an o1-based annotation method to identify all errors in a trace, then scoring parent-child induction likelihood via few-shot LLM prompting to build error trees, with static metrics (forest size, nodes/tree, depth/tree) and a dynamic metric (Average Error Node Reproduction Rate, Repro) characterizing forest growth. Five key observations emerge: (1) rectifying only child/grandchild error nodes causes the parent to keep spawning new offspring, while correcting the root node significantly decelerates error generation, revealing a parent-child dependency where root nodes drive growth; (2) FoE's scale in First is substantially smaller than in Subs (forest depth in Subs exceeds First by ~16.3%, reproduction rate 33.3% lower in First); (3) root-node (and more generally error-node) generation is jointly driven by high token entropy AND high entropy variance in a sliding window -- neither alone suffices; (4) LRMs' self-reflection largely fails to prune FoE, and reflection frequency/completeness/depth all decline sharply from First to later Subs (e.g. 62.5% frequency reduction, 68.2% completeness reduction, 82.1% depth reduction for Qwen3-8B-thinking), with fake correction (superficial edits that leave the original erroneous logic intact) and refusal to correct together displacing true correction as the dominant behavior in Subs (64.2%/31.1% vs. 32.4%/0.5% in First). Building on these findings, proposes RED (Refine First, Discard Subs): (I) Refining First monitors a sliding window of token entropy and entropy variance during First's generation; when the window's entropy variance exceeds threshold T and the next token's entropy exceeds the window's recorded average top-K entropy (the joint high-high condition identified as root-error-prone), a classifier-free-guidance-style intervention appends a concise negative prompt ('No, I made a mistake.') after the stored KV cache to generate a negative-branch logit distribution, then subtracts (with tunable coefficient alpha) this negative branch's log-probabilities from the original next-token distribution, steering generation away from the erroneous trajectory at exactly the segments prone to root-error genesis; (II) Discarding Subs entirely forgoes generating alternative solutions, instead probing every K steps with M parallel prompt templates (N samples each) for interim answers and triggering early exit once a dual-consistency condition holds (internal consistency: the dominant answer within each template appears with frequency >= P%; cross-prompt agreement: the dominant answers across all M templates are identical), avoiding both the cost and the error-propagation risk of full Subs generation. Evaluated across Qwen3-8B/32B-thinking, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B/70B on AIME24/25, MATH500, GSM8K, GPQA-Diamond against Vanilla, DEER, Think or Not, AlphaOne, DAST, RL+LP, GRPO, S-GRPO.
methods: DEER / Think or Not / AlphaOne / DAST / RL+LP / GRPO / S-GRPO (baselines)
one_liner: Discovers 'The First is The Best' -- across five reasoning benchmarks and multiple LRMs, a model's first-generated solution is optimal in up to 93.7% of cases, because reasoning errors form a self-propagating forest structure (Forest of Errors, FoE) that grows faster and larger in subsequent solutions than in the first -- then proposes RED (Refine First, Discard Subs), which entropy-triggers negative-prompt intervention only on the first solution's root-error-prone segments and prunes all subsequent solutions via a dual-consistency early-stop check, improving accuracy up to 19.0% while cutting tokens 37.7-70.4% across six backbones and five benchmarks.
problem: Large reasoning models trained via RL exhibit an 'aha-moment' pattern of exploring multiple alternative solutions, widely assumed (per standard test-time-scaling laws) to be beneficial, but this exploration substantially inflates chain-of-thought length and computational cost, raising the question of whether exploring multiple solutions is actually necessary or whether it is instead a source of wasted (or actively harmful) computation.

relevance.overthinking: Directly central to the topic and among the most consequential findings in this archive: it directly challenges the standard test-time-scaling assumption that exploring more alternative solutions helps, with hard numbers showing a model's own alternative solutions actively make things worse in a substantial fraction of cases (up to 21.2% of correct-first cases turned wrong). The Forest of Errors framework gives a structural, mechanistic account of exactly how and why overthinking-via-exploration backfires -- errors self-propagate and grow faster in later solutions -- complementing this archive's other mechanistic accounts (NeuReasoner's Mixture of Neurons, DOT's length shift, DTSR's reflection-signal overconfidence) with a distinct forest/tree-structured lens on error genesis, and its finding that self-reflection increasingly degrades into 'fake correction' in later solutions is a sharp, quantified explanation for why naive reflection-suppression methods (like NOWAIT, shown to hurt accuracy in other papers here) may be removing exactly the wrong thing.

results: RED strikes the best performance-efficiency balance across almost all six backbones and five benchmarks, generally improving accuracy 0.3-5.6 points (3.2-19.0% relative) over Vanilla while cutting token consumption 37.7-70.4% -- e.g. on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B+AIME25, RED achieves the largest single margin: +5.5 score with 56.4% token reduction, outperforming all eight baselines. RED consistently beats the strongest RL-based competitor tested, S-GRPO, by margins up to 3.3 points in accuracy and 7.1 percentage points in additional token efficiency (e.g. Qwen3-32B-thinking/AIME25: RED 72.2/S-GRPO 71.1 accuracy, RED 5908/S-GRPO 6389 tokens). Scalability analysis on the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama series shows DAST's performance gain degrades from +3.3 at 8B to -2.2 at 70B relative to Vanilla, while RED remains robust, achieving +5.5 and +2.2 gains respectively -- indicating RED's mechanism (targeting the entropy-signature of error genesis directly, rather than a learned length-reward policy) generalizes better across scale than the RL-based alternative. FoE-metric evaluation (Table 4, AIME25) confirms RED achieves substantial, mechanism-level pruning of the forest itself: reducing all FoE metrics by 41.0-68.0%, versus the strongest competing baseline (S-GRPO) which only reduces the dynamic Repro metric by 7.4% and the static D/T metric by a negligible 3.4% on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B -- directly demonstrating RED addresses the underlying error-generation mechanism rather than only its token-count symptom. A rigorous latency stress test (isolating RED's intervention overhead by disabling early-exit while keeping the periodic probing and entropy-based intervention active) shows the additional per-step latency overhead averages only 4.6%, far outweighed by the time saved from early exit, yielding a net inference speedup versus baseline.
